# Timing Sprocket Marks Disagree with Distributor for TDC

You have turned the crankshaft so that both the camshaft sprocket dot is at the bottom and the crankshaft sprocket dot is at the top. This configuration represents the factory-defined Top Dead Center (TDC) for cylinder 1 on your 3.9L V6 engine. However, when you observe the distributor, it indicates that cylinder 4 is firing instead of cylinder 1. Conversely, if you rotate the engine until the distributor signals a cylinder 1 event, the timing marks on the sprockets will no longer align with their specified TDC positions.

This discrepancy usually points to one of two fundamental issues: an incorrect distributor installation or a misunderstanding of the firing order relative to the physical location of the distributor shaft. In many modern engines, including later iterations of this platform, the distributor is not a fixed component but rather a removable unit that can be rotated on its shaft. If the previous owner installed the distributor without rotating it to match the specific timing marks for cylinder 1 at TDC, you are now seeing a mismatch between the internal camshaft position and the external ignition signal.

To verify the state of your engine, you must first ensure the ignition system is safe to work on. Disconnect the negative battery terminal and remove the distributor cap. Rotate the crankshaft using a breaker bar on the crankshaft pulley bolt until the timing marks align perfectly as specified in the manual: cam dot down, crank dot up.

At this exact moment, observe the position of the rotor inside the distributor housing. On a standard configuration for this engine family, the rotor should be pointing directly toward the terminal that connects to the number 1 spark plug wire when viewed from above. If the rotor is pointing toward any other terminal, the distributor shaft has been rotated relative to the camshaft position.

It is critical to distinguish between a simple misalignment and a mechanical error in the timing set itself. The scenario where the marks align at TDC but the engine runs poorly often suggests a vacuum leak or an ignition component failure, such as a fouled spark plug or coil pack. However, if the marks do not align when you try to force the distributor to fire cylinder 1, the issue is strictly rotational alignment of the distributor cap.

The solution involves removing the distributor. Once removed, rotate the shaft until the rotor points correctly at the number 1 terminal while the engine remains at TDC (cam dot down, crank dot up). Reinstall the distributor without applying excessive torque to the hold-down bolt initially; allow the shaft to float freely so that the internal gears can mesh properly with the camshaft. Only tighten the hold-down bolt once you have confirmed the alignment is correct and the distributor is seated fully against its gasket.

Be aware that rotating a distributor 180 degrees effectively reverses the firing order relative to the physical terminals on the cap. This could lead to misfires, rough idling, or difficulty starting if not corrected immediately. The fact that your truck runs "rough but not terrible" is consistent with an ignition system firing in the wrong sequence rather than a catastrophic engine failure. While a bad catalytic converter can cause performance issues, it will not alter the mechanical relationship between the timing marks and the distributor shaft.

If you are working on a platform where software diagnostics play a role, understanding these mechanical baselines is essential before attempting to write custom logic or diagnostic scripts. For instance, if you were building a monitoring dashboard for vehicle telemetry, your code would need to account for this physical offset rather than assuming TDC always corresponds to a specific sensor reading without calibration.

After reseating the distributor and reconnecting all wiring, verify the alignment one final time before starting the engine. If the marks align at TDC and the rotor points to cylinder 1, the timing set itself is likely fine, and the previous owner simply missed the critical step of rotating the distributor shaft during reinstallation.
